concepts.difficultyReason: Topic complexity and original course position (Book 2, chapter 21); editorial estimate.
concepts.title: Arabic groups words into three parts of speech
concepts.rule: Use the Arabic categories: اِسْمٌ، فِعْلٌ، حَرْفٌ.
concepts.note: Read this rule with the conditions and examples in its original explanation.

sourceCards.title: Arabic groups words into three parts of speech
sourceCards.takeaway: Use the Arabic categories: اِسْمٌ، فِعْلٌ، حَرْفٌ.

examples.arabic:
الِاسْمُ: كِتَابٌ، هُوَ، أَنَا، هَذَا، قَبْلَ
الْفِعْلُ: كَتَبَ، يَكْتُبُ، اُكْتُبْ، لَيْسَ
الْحَرْفُ: مَا، لَا، نَعَمْ، لَمْ، سَـ
examples.translation:
Ism: book, he, I, this, before
Fil: he wrote, he writes, write!, is not
Harf: ma, la, yes, lam, future sa-
examples.explanation: The Arabic category اِسْمٌ is broader than the everyday English idea of a naming noun: it includes pronouns and demonstratives. A فِعْلٌ is a verb, including the past, present-future and command forms shown. A حَرْفٌ is a particle with a grammatical function; here the term does not mean a single alphabet letter.

reviewPrompts.prompt: Name the three Arabic parts of speech and give one example of each.
reviewPrompts.answer: اِسْمٌ (ism), فِعْلٌ (fil), حَرْفٌ (harf). Examples: كِتَابٌ, كَتَبَ, and لَمْ respectively.

examples.arabic: هَذَا كِتَابٌ
examples.translation: This is a book.
examples.explanation: The first “a” sound in هَذَا is long, even though a full alif is not written there. The small alif above the letter helps show that long sound.

concepts.title: You can leave “is” unsaid
concepts.rule: Two words can make a complete Arabic sentence.
concepts.note: Read this rule with the conditions and examples in its original explanation.

sourceCards.title: You can leave “is” unsaid
sourceCards.takeaway: Two words can make a complete Arabic sentence.

examples.arabic: هَذَا كِتَابٌ
examples.translation: This is a book.
examples.explanation: هَذَا means “this” and كِتَابٌ means “a book.” Together they already make a complete statement. English needs “is” in the translation; this Arabic sentence does not.

reviewPrompts.answer: Two words can make a complete Arabic sentence.

concepts.title: Recognize an indefinite noun
concepts.rule: For ordinary nouns such as كِتَابٌ, tanwin accompanies an indefinite meaning: “a book.”
concepts.note: An introductory pattern, not a definition of every word with tanwin.

sourceCards.title: Where is the word “a”?
sourceCards.takeaway: For these nouns, the ending helps express “a” or “an.”

examples.arabic: كِتَابٌ   ·   بَيْتٌ   ·   مَسْجِدٌ
examples.translation: A book · a house · a mosque
examples.explanation: This ending is called tanwin. Here, the double vowel mark ٌ is read “un.” It tells you that the noun is indefinite: a book, rather than a particular book. Later, you will see tanwin on other kinds of words too.

reviewPrompts.prompt: What does كِتَابٌ mean in this example?
reviewPrompts.answer: A book.

concepts.title: Turn a statement into a question
concepts.rule: A small أَ at the start changes the statement into a question.
concepts.note: Read this rule with the conditions and examples in its original explanation.

sourceCards.title: Turn a statement into a question
sourceCards.takeaway: A small أَ at the start changes the statement into a question.

examples.arabic: هَذَا بَيْتٌ ← أَهَذَا بَيْتٌ؟
examples.translation: This is a house. → Is this a house?
examples.explanation: The rest of the sentence stays the same. You can answer with نَعَمْ (“yes”) or لَا (“no”). The lesson also introduces مَا هَذَا؟ (“What is this?”) and مَنْ هَذَا؟ (“Who is this?”).

reviewPrompts.arabic: هَذَا بَيْتٌ ← أَهَذَا بَيْتٌ؟
reviewPrompts.answer: A small أَ at the start changes the statement into a question.
reviewPrompts.translation: This is a house. → Is this a house?

concepts.title: From “this” to “that”
concepts.rule: هَذَا points near; ذَلِكَ points farther away.
concepts.note: Read this rule with the conditions and examples in its original explanation.

sourceCards.title: From “this” to “that”
sourceCards.takeaway: هَذَا points near; ذَلِكَ points farther away.

examples.arabic: هَذَا بَيْتٌ وَذَلِكَ مَسْجِدٌ
examples.translation: This is a house and that is a mosque.
examples.explanation: Like هَذَا, ذَلِكَ has a long “a” sound that is not written with a full alif. The small alif in a fully marked text helps you read it. Both words refer to masculine nouns in this lesson.

reviewPrompts.prompt: Explain what is being pointed out and how the demonstrative form or placement works.

concepts.title: Join two ideas with “and”
concepts.rule: Write وَ together with the next word.
concepts.note: Read this rule with the conditions and examples in its original explanation.

sourceCards.title: Join two ideas with “and”
sourceCards.takeaway: Write وَ together with the next word.

examples.arabic: هَذَا بَيْتٌ وَذَلِكَ مَسْجِدٌ
examples.translation: This is a house and that is a mosque.
examples.explanation: Notice وَذَلِكَ in the example. There is no space between وَ and ذَلِكَ. The joining word lets you connect two statements you already know how to make.

reviewPrompts.arabic: هَذَا بَيْتٌ وَذَلِكَ مَسْجِدٌ
reviewPrompts.answer: Write وَ together with the next word.
reviewPrompts.translation: This is a house and that is a mosque.

concepts.title: Make a noun definite with الـ
concepts.rule: Add الـ and remove tanwin: بَيْتٌ becomes الْبَيْتُ.
concepts.note: The example is nominative; الـ does not determine the noun’s case.

sourceCards.title: Make “a house” into “the house”
sourceCards.takeaway: Add الـ and remove tanwin: a noun becomes definite.

examples.arabic: بَيْتٌ ← الْبَيْتُ
examples.translation: A house → the house
examples.explanation: When الـ is added, the tanwin ending goes away. Compare بَيْتٌ, ending in “un,” with الْبَيْتُ, ending in “u.” Do not keep both الـ and tanwin on the same noun in this pattern.

reviewPrompts.prompt: Change بَيْتٌ (“a house”) to “the house.”
reviewPrompts.answer: الْبَيْتُ. Add الـ and replace tanwin with the appropriate single case vowel.

concepts.title: Sun letters borrow the lām sound
concepts.rule: Keep الـ in writing; double the sun letter in speech.
concepts.note: Read this rule with the conditions and examples in its original explanation.

sourceCards.title: Sun letters borrow the lām sound
sourceCards.takeaway: Keep الـ in writing; double the sun letter in speech.

examples.arabic: الشَّمْسُ
examples.translation: The sun
examples.explanation: This is pronounced “ash-shamsu,” rather than “al-shamsu.” The ل stays in the spelling. A shaddah on ش marks the doubled sound. The book also gives النَّجْمُ (the star), الدِّيكُ (the rooster), الرَّجُلُ (the man), and السَّمَكُ (the fish).

reviewPrompts.prompt: Read this aloud. What sound changes in connected speech, and why?
reviewPrompts.arabic: الشَّمْسُ
reviewPrompts.answer: Keep الـ in writing; double the sun letter in speech.
reviewPrompts.translation: The sun

concepts.title: Moon letters let the lām be heard
concepts.rule: With a moon letter, keep the “l” sound of al.
concepts.note: Read this rule with the conditions and examples in its original explanation.

sourceCards.title: Moon letters let the lām be heard
sourceCards.takeaway: With a moon letter, keep the “l” sound of al.

examples.arabic: الْقَمَرُ
examples.translation: The moon
examples.explanation: Read this as “al-qamaru.” Arabic has 14 sun letters and 14 moon letters. The sun letters are ت ث د ذ ر ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ل ن; the remaining letters are moon letters. Compare الشَّمْسُ with الْقَمَرُ to hear the difference.

reviewPrompts.arabic: الْقَمَرُ
reviewPrompts.answer: With a moon letter, keep the “l” sound of al.

concepts.title: Let words flow into الـ
concepts.rule: The spelling stays; the opening vowel joins smoothly to the previous word.
concepts.note: Read this rule with the conditions and examples in its original explanation.

sourceCards.title: Let words flow into الـ
sourceCards.takeaway: The spelling stays; the opening vowel joins smoothly to the previous word.

examples.arabic: الْبَيْتُ   ←   وَالْبَيْتُ
examples.translation: The house → and the house
examples.explanation: Read الْبَيْتُ on its own as “al-baytu.” With وَ before it, read وَالْبَيْتُ as “wal-baytu.” The alif remains in writing. This connecting initial vowel is called hamzat al-wasl; the sign ٱ can mark it.

reviewPrompts.arabic: الْبَيْتُ   ←   وَالْبَيْتُ
reviewPrompts.answer: The spelling stays; the opening vowel joins smoothly to the previous word.
reviewPrompts.translation: The house → and the house

concepts.title: A noun’s ending tells you its job
concepts.rule: Pay attention to the final vowel, not just the letters of the word.
concepts.note: Read this rule with the conditions and examples in its original explanation.

sourceCards.title: A noun’s ending tells you its job
sourceCards.takeaway: Pay attention to the final vowel, not just the letters of the word.

examples.arabic: الْبَيْتُ جَدِيدٌ
examples.translation: The house is new.
examples.explanation: الْبَيْتُ ends with a dammah, the short “u” vowel. The Key calls a noun in this state marfuʿ. For now, notice this ending; in the next card, you will see how a preposition changes it.

reviewPrompts.prompt: Explain the grammatical roles here and how their case is shown.
reviewPrompts.arabic: الْبَيْتُ جَدِيدٌ
reviewPrompts.answer: Pay attention to the final vowel, not just the letters of the word.
reviewPrompts.translation: The house is new.

concepts.title: After “in” or “on,” the ending changes
concepts.rule: After a preposition, look for the “i” ending in these examples.
concepts.note: Read this rule with the conditions and examples in its original explanation.

sourceCards.title: After “in” or “on,” the ending changes
sourceCards.takeaway: After a preposition, look for the “i” ending in these examples.

examples.arabic:
فِي الْبَيْتِ
عَلَى الْمَكْتَبِ
فِي بَيْتٍ
examples.translation:
In the house
On the table
In a house
examples.explanation: Compare الْبَيْتُ with فِي الْبَيْتِ: the ending changes from “u” to “i.” An indefinite noun keeps tanwin, but “un” changes to “in”: بَيْتٌ becomes بَيْتٍ. These are the patterns for the nouns shown here.

reviewPrompts.prompt: Identify the preposition and explain its meaning or effect on its complement.
reviewPrompts.arabic:
فِي الْبَيْتِ
عَلَى الْمَكْتَبِ
فِي بَيْتٍ
reviewPrompts.answer: After a preposition, look for the “i” ending in these examples.
reviewPrompts.translation:
In the house
On the table
In a house

concepts.title: A shorter vowel when فِي meets الـ
concepts.rule: Write فِي الْبَيْتِ; connect it in speech as “fil-bayti.”
concepts.note: Read this rule with the conditions and examples in its original explanation.

sourceCards.title: A shorter vowel when فِي meets الـ
sourceCards.takeaway: Write فِي الْبَيْتِ; connect it in speech as “fil-bayti.”

examples.arabic:
فِي بَيْتٍ
فِي الْبَيْتِ
examples.translation:
In a house
In the house
examples.explanation: In فِي بَيْتٍ, keep the long vowel of fi. In فِي الْبَيْتِ, read the connection as “fil-bayti.” You already learned that the initial vowel of الـ drops after a preceding word; here the long vowel of فِي is shortened too. The spelling stays the same.

reviewPrompts.prompt: Read this aloud. What sound changes in connected speech, and why?
reviewPrompts.arabic:
فِي بَيْتٍ
فِي الْبَيْتِ
reviewPrompts.answer: Write فِي الْبَيْتِ; connect it in speech as “fil-bayti.”
reviewPrompts.translation:
In a house
In the house

concepts.title: “He” and “she” can also mean “it”
concepts.rule: Choose هُوَ or هِيَ according to the Arabic noun’s gender.
concepts.note: Read this rule with the conditions and examples in its original explanation.

sourceCards.title: “He” and “she” can also mean “it”
sourceCards.takeaway: Choose هُوَ or هِيَ according to the Arabic noun’s gender.

examples.arabic:
أَيْنَ الْكِتَابُ؟ هُوَ عَلَى الْمَكْتَبِ
أَيْنَ السَّاعَةُ؟ هِيَ عَلَى السَّرِيرِ
examples.translation:
Where is the book? It is on the table.
Where is the watch? It is on the bed.
examples.explanation: Arabic nouns have grammatical gender. كِتَابٌ is masculine, so use هُوَ. سَاعَةٌ is feminine, so use هِيَ. Most feminine nouns end in ة, but some do not. Learn a noun’s gender along with its meaning.

reviewPrompts.prompt: Identify what each pronoun refers to and explain the distinction illustrated.
reviewPrompts.arabic:
أَيْنَ الْكِتَابُ؟ هُوَ عَلَى الْمَكْتَبِ
أَيْنَ السَّاعَةُ؟ هِيَ عَلَى السَّرِيرِ
reviewPrompts.answer: Choose هُوَ or هِيَ according to the Arabic noun’s gender.
reviewPrompts.translation:
Where is the book? It is on the table.
Where is the watch? It is on the bed.

concepts.title: Put the thing before its owner
concepts.rule: In an ordinary possessive idafah, put the thing first and the owner second: كِتَابُ بِلَالٍ.
concepts.note: Mudaf = first noun; mudaf ilayhi = complement. Idafah can express relationships beyond ownership.

sourceCards.title: Put the thing before its owner
sourceCards.takeaway: Thing first, owner second: “book of Bilal.”

examples.arabic:
كِتَابُ بِلَالٍ
بَيْتُ الْإِمَامِ
examples.translation:
Bilal’s book
The imam’s house
examples.explanation: The first word is the thing possessed, called the mudaf. The second is the possessor, called the mudaf ilayhi. Together they form an idafah, a possession or “of” construction. There is no separate apostrophe or word for “of.”

reviewPrompts.prompt: Say “Bilal’s book” using كِتَاب and بِلَال.
reviewPrompts.answer: كِتَابُ بِلَالٍ: thing first, owner second.

concepts.title: A connecting vowel beyond الـ
concepts.rule: Hamzat al-wasl drops in connected speech in اِسْمٌ and اِبْنٌ too.
concepts.note: Read this rule with the conditions and examples in its original explanation.

sourceCards.title: A connecting vowel beyond الـ
sourceCards.takeaway: Hamzat al-wasl drops in connected speech in اِسْمٌ and اِبْنٌ too.

examples.arabic:
اِسْمُ الْوَلَدِ بِلَالٌ، وَاسْمُ الْبِنْتِ آمِنَةُ
أَيْنَ ابْنُ حَامِدٍ؟
examples.translation:
The boy’s name is Bilal, and the girl’s name is Aminah.
Where is Hamid’s son?
examples.explanation: At the start of speech, pronounce the initial “i” in ism or ibn. When another word comes before it, omit that vowel in connected speech: وَاسْمُ is read “wasmu,” and أَيْنَ ابْنُ is connected as “ayna-bnu.” The initial alif stays in writing.

reviewPrompts.prompt: Read this aloud. What sound changes in connected speech, and why?
reviewPrompts.arabic:
اِسْمُ الْوَلَدِ بِلَالٌ، وَاسْمُ الْبِنْتِ آمِنَةُ
أَيْنَ ابْنُ حَامِدٍ؟
reviewPrompts.answer: Hamzat al-wasl drops in connected speech in اِسْمٌ and اِبْنٌ too.
reviewPrompts.translation:
The boy’s name is Bilal, and the girl’s name is Aminah.

concepts.title: A feminine word for “this”
concepts.rule: Match “this” to the noun: هَذَا for masculine, هَذِهِ for feminine.
concepts.note: Read this rule with the conditions and examples in its original explanation.

sourceCards.title: A feminine word for “this”
sourceCards.takeaway: Match “this” to the noun: هَذَا for masculine, هَذِهِ for feminine.

examples.arabic: هَذَا وَلَدٌ وَهَذِهِ بِنْتٌ
examples.translation: This is a boy and this is a girl.
examples.explanation: وَلَدٌ is masculine, so it goes with هَذَا. بِنْتٌ is feminine, so it goes with هَذِهِ. Like هَذَا, هَذِهِ has a long first “a” sound without a full alif in its spelling.

reviewPrompts.arabic: هَذَا وَلَدٌ وَهَذِهِ بِنْتٌ
reviewPrompts.answer: Match “this” to the noun: هَذَا for masculine, هَذِهِ for feminine.
reviewPrompts.translation: This is a boy and this is a girl.

concepts.title: A common feminine ending: ة
concepts.rule: Look for a short “a” before the feminine ending ة.
concepts.note: Read this rule with the conditions and examples in its original explanation.

sourceCards.title: A common feminine ending: ة
sourceCards.takeaway: Look for a short “a” before the feminine ending ة.

examples.arabic: مُدَرِّسٌ ← مُدَرِّسَةٌ
examples.translation: A male teacher → a female teacher
examples.explanation: The feminine form is read “mudarrisatun” when its ending is pronounced. The ة is called ta marbutah. This is a common pattern, not a way to change every noun: some words have a separate feminine form.

reviewPrompts.arabic: مُدَرِّسٌ ← مُدَرِّسَةٌ
reviewPrompts.answer: Look for a short “a” before the feminine ending ة.
reviewPrompts.translation: A male teacher → a female teacher

concepts.title: Sometimes the feminine word is different
concepts.rule: Learn the gender with the word; ة is a useful clue, not a universal rule.
concepts.note: Read this rule with the conditions and examples in its original explanation.

sourceCards.title: Sometimes the feminine word is different
sourceCards.takeaway: Learn the gender with the word; ة is a useful clue, not a universal rule.

examples.arabic:
اِبْنٌ   ·   بِنْتٌ
أَخٌ   ·   أُخْتٌ
examples.translation:
Son · daughter
Brother · sister
examples.explanation: Learn each pair together. بِنْتٌ and أُخْتٌ are feminine even though neither ends in ة. A noun’s meaning and learned gender matter more than guessing from its last letter.

أَخٌ   ·   أُخْتٌ

concepts.title: Gender is not always visible
concepts.rule: A feminine noun does not need a ة ending.
concepts.note: Read this rule with the conditions and examples in its original explanation.

sourceCards.title: Gender is not always visible
sourceCards.takeaway: A feminine noun does not need a ة ending.

examples.arabic:
يَدٌ   ·   عَيْنٌ
رَأْسٌ   ·   أَنْفٌ
examples.translation:
Hand · eye (feminine)
Head · nose (masculine)
examples.explanation: The feminine examples are يَدٌ (hand), رِجْلٌ (leg), عَيْنٌ (eye), and أُذُنٌ (ear). The masculine examples are رَأْسٌ (head), أَنْفٌ (nose), فَمٌ (mouth), and وَجْهٌ (face). Treat this as a learning aid and learn each noun’s gender.

reviewPrompts.arabic:
يَدٌ   ·   عَيْنٌ
رَأْسٌ   ·   أَنْفٌ
reviewPrompts.answer: A feminine noun does not need a ة ending.
reviewPrompts.translation:
Hand · eye (feminine)
Head · nose (masculine)

sourceCards.takeaway: Attach لِـ to the next noun and use its majrur form.

concepts.rule: Use جَلَسَ for “he sat,” and add a location to say where.
concepts.note: Read this rule with the conditions and examples in its original explanation.

sourceCards.title: A new action: “he sat”
sourceCards.takeaway: Use جَلَسَ for “he sat,” and add a location to say where.

examples.arabic:
أَيْنَ جَلَسَ مُحَمَّدٌ؟
جَلَسَ أَمَامَ الْمُدَرِّسِ
examples.translation:
Where did Muhammad sit?
He sat in front of the teacher.
examples.explanation: أَيْنَ asks “where.” In the question, مُحَمَّدٌ names the person who sat. In the answer, جَلَسَ already carries the meaning “he sat,” so there is no need to repeat the name. This follows the verb pattern introduced with ذَهَبَ in Lesson 4a.

concepts.title: Match the noun’s grammatical gender
concepts.rule: A describing adjective agrees with its noun in grammatical gender, even when the noun has no ة.
concepts.note: Assumes basic recognition of masculine and feminine nouns.

sourceCards.title: Match the adjective to the noun’s gender
sourceCards.takeaway: Match grammatical gender, rather than just copying the noun’s last letter.

examples.arabic:
وَلَدٌ صَغِيرٌ   ·   بِنْتٌ صَغِيرَةٌ
كِتَابٌ جَدِيدٌ   ·   سَيَّارَةٌ جَدِيدَةٌ
examples.translation:
A small boy · a small girl
A new book · a new car
examples.explanation: صَغِيرٌ becomes صَغِيرَةٌ with بِنْتٌ. جَدِيدٌ becomes جَدِيدَةٌ with سَيَّارَةٌ. Notice that بِنْتٌ is feminine without ة, while its adjective still uses the feminine form.

reviewPrompts.prompt: Choose: بِنْتٌ صَغِيرٌ or بِنْتٌ صَغِيرَةٌ?
reviewPrompts.answer: بِنْتٌ صَغِيرَةٌ. بِنْتٌ is feminine although it has no ة.

concepts.title: Match definiteness in a describing phrase
concepts.rule: A describing adjective follows its noun and matches its definiteness. For an ordinary noun made definite with الـ, its describing adjective takes الـ too.
concepts.note: The later review restates word order and definiteness together. Keep the adjective/predicate contrast separate.

sourceCards.title: Match “the” on the adjective too
sourceCards.takeaway: For “the new teacher,” both the noun and its describing adjective take الـ.

sourceCards.title: An adjective follows its noun and matches definiteness
sourceCards.takeaway: A describing adjective follows its noun and matches its definiteness.

examples.arabic:
بِلَالٌ مُدَرِّسٌ جَدِيدٌ
الْمُدَرِّسُ الْجَدِيدُ فِي الْفَصْلِ
examples.translation:
Bilal is a new teacher.
The new teacher is in the classroom.
examples.explanation: مُدَرِّسٌ جَدِيدٌ has no الـ on either word. الْمُدَرِّسُ الْجَدِيدُ has الـ on both. Compare الْمُدَرِّسُ جَدِيدٌ: that is the statement “The teacher is new,” rather than the phrase “the new teacher.”

examples.arabic:
هَذَا كِتَابٌ جَدِيدٌ.
الْكِتَابُ الْجَدِيدُ سَهْلٌ.
examples.translation:
This is a new book.
The new book is easy.
examples.explanation: In the first sentence, كِتَابٌ and جَدِيدٌ are both indefinite. In the second, الْكِتَابُ and الْجَدِيدُ are both definite. سَهْلٌ is the predicate, not another definite adjective inside “the new book.” This final chapter reviews four dimensions of adjective agreement.

reviewPrompts.prompt: Say “the new teacher.”
reviewPrompts.answer: الْمُدَرِّسُ الْجَدِيدُ.

concepts.title: Distinguish a description from a statement
concepts.rule: الْمُدَرِّسُ الْجَدِيدُ means “the new teacher”; الْمُدَرِّسُ جَدِيدٌ means “the teacher is new.”
concepts.note: A comparison assembled from two cards, not a claim that the cards are duplicates. These examples do not make every predicate indefinite.

sourceCards.title: Match “the” on the adjective too
sourceCards.takeaway: For “the new teacher,” both the noun and its describing adjective take الـ.

sourceCards.title: Tanwin does not always mean “a”
sourceCards.takeaway: On these describing words, tanwin does not add an English “a.”

examples.arabic:
بِلَالٌ مُدَرِّسٌ جَدِيدٌ
الْمُدَرِّسُ الْجَدِيدُ فِي الْفَصْلِ
examples.translation:
Bilal is a new teacher.
The new teacher is in the classroom.
examples.explanation: مُدَرِّسٌ جَدِيدٌ has no الـ on either word. الْمُدَرِّسُ الْجَدِيدُ has الـ on both. Compare الْمُدَرِّسُ جَدِيدٌ: that is the statement “The teacher is new,” rather than the phrase “the new teacher.”

examples.arabic:
الْبَابُ مَفْتُوحٌ
الْقَلَمُ مَكْسُورٌ
examples.translation:
The door is open.
The pen is broken.
examples.explanation: مَفْتُوحٌ describes something as “open,” and مَكْسُورٌ describes something as “broken.” Both have tanwin, but English does not say “a open” or “a broken” here. Translate the meaning of the whole sentence.

reviewPrompts.prompt: Which is a statement: الْمُدَرِّسُ الْجَدِيدُ or الْمُدَرِّسُ جَدِيدٌ?
reviewPrompts.answer: الْمُدَرِّسُ جَدِيدٌ: “The teacher is new.” The indefinite word is the predicate here.

concepts.rule: Tanwin is an ending, not an English word: مَفْتُوحٌ in this predicate means “open,” not “a open.”

concepts.title: A name can be definite and have tanwin
concepts.rule: A proper name such as حَامِدٌ identifies a person and is definite even though it has tanwin.
concepts.note: Separate from predicate translation: this addresses definiteness itself.

sourceCards.title: A name can have tanwin too
sourceCards.takeaway: Translate the name itself; do not add “a” because of tanwin.

examples.arabic: حَامِدٌ
examples.translation: Hamid
examples.explanation: You first saw tanwin in بَيْتٌ, “a house.” But حَامِدٌ is simply “Hamid,” never “a Hamid” in this lesson. Like the describing words from Chapter 3, names show why tanwin cannot always be translated as “a.”

reviewPrompts.prompt: Does حَامِدٌ mean “a Hamid” because it has tanwin?
reviewPrompts.answer: No. It is the name Hamid; a proper name is definite.

concepts.rule: The feminine names illustrated here take a single dammah, not tanwin, in the nominative. Their gender need not be shown by ة.

sourceCards.title: Review: feminine proper names without tanwin

examples.translation: Fatimah · Zaynab · Aminah

examples.arabic: آمِنَةُ   ·   زَيْنَبُ
examples.translation: Aminah · Zaynab

concepts.rule: In these فَعْلَان adjectives, the written ن is part of the word. The illustrated forms have no tanwin.
concepts.note: The later chapter repeats the same illustrated adjective pattern. Its source and examples remain attached.

sourceCards.title: The “n” here is not tanwin
sourceCards.takeaway: For these -ān adjectives, keep the written ن and use no tanwin.

sourceCards.title: Review: adjectives on فَعْلَان
sourceCards.takeaway: فَعْلَان adjectives such as كَسْلَانُ have no tanwin here.

examples.arabic:
كَسْلَانُ   ·   جَوْعَانُ   ·   عَطْشَانُ
غَضْبَانُ   ·   مَلْآنُ
examples.translation:
Lazy · hungry · thirsty
Angry · full
examples.explanation: These words have a written ن as part of the word itself. Their ending here is a single dammah, “u,” not the double dammah of tanwin. Do not confuse the long “ān” inside the word with an added tanwin “n.”

examples.arabic: كَسْلَانُ   ·   مَلْآنُ
examples.translation: Lazy · full
examples.explanation: This collects the pattern introduced in Chapter 9, which also included جَوْعَانُ, عَطْشَانُ, and غَضْبَانُ. The final ن belongs to the word itself; the case form shown has a single dammah.

concepts.title: Identify someone with “who…”
concepts.rule: Use the “who…” clause to identify the person before giving the main information.
concepts.note: Read this rule with the conditions and examples in its original explanation.

sourceCards.title: Identify someone with “who…”
sourceCards.source: Part B · Point 2 · Human example · p. 22
sourceCards.takeaway: Use the “who…” clause to identify the person before giving the main information.

examples.arabic: الرَّجُلُ الَّذِي خَرَجَ مِنَ الْمَسْجِدِ الْآنَ تَاجِرٌ شَهِيرٌ
examples.translation: The man who went out of the mosque just now is a famous merchant.
examples.explanation: الرَّجُلُ names the person. الَّذِي خَرَجَ مِنَ الْمَسْجِدِ الْآنَ tells you which man. تَاجِرٌ شَهِيرٌ tells you something about him. Take the sentence in those three pieces to understand its structure.

reviewPrompts.answer: Use the “who…” clause to identify the person before giving the main information.
reviewPrompts.translation: The man who went out of the mosque just now is a famous merchant.

concepts.title: The same الَّذِي can mean “which”
concepts.rule: Translate الَّذِي according to what it refers to: “who” for a person, “which” for a thing.
concepts.note: Read this rule with the conditions and examples in its original explanation.

sourceCards.title: The same الَّذِي can mean “which”
sourceCards.source: Part B · Point 2 · Thing example · p. 22
sourceCards.takeaway: Translate الَّذِي according to what it refers to: “who” for a person, “which” for a thing.

examples.arabic: الْبَيْتُ الَّذِي أَمَامَ الْمَسْجِدِ لِلْإِمَامِ
examples.translation: The house which is in front of the mosque belongs to the imam.
examples.explanation: الَّذِي أَمَامَ الْمَسْجِدِ identifies which house. لِلْإِمَامِ gives the main information: it belongs to the imam. كِتَابٌ and بَيْتٌ are grammatically masculine, so a masculine form can refer to a thing. Other relative-pronoun forms come later.

reviewPrompts.translation: The house which is in front of the mosque belongs to the imam.

concepts.title: Attach “your,” “his,” and “her”
concepts.rule: Attached pronouns can fill the owner’s place: كِتَابُكَ, كِتَابُهُ, كِتَابُهَا. The first noun has no الـ or tanwin.
concepts.note: ـكَ addresses one male person; ـهُ is “his” and ـهَا is “her.”

sourceCards.title: Attach “your,” “his,” and “her” to the noun
sourceCards.takeaway: Attach the owner: كِتَابُ + ـكَ becomes كِتَابُكَ.

examples.arabic: كِتَابُكَ   ·   كِتَابُهُ   ·   كِتَابُهَا
examples.translation: Your book (one male person) · his book · her book
examples.explanation: ـكَ means “your” when addressing one male person, ـهُ means “his,” and ـهَا means “her.” These are attached pronouns, rather than separate words. They fill the owner’s place in the idafah pattern, so the noun has neither الـ nor tanwin.

reviewPrompts.prompt: How do you say “her book”?
reviewPrompts.answer: كِتَابُهَا.

concepts.title: Use the long ī ending for “my”
concepts.rule: كِتَابِي means “my book.” Read a long final ī rather than the u heard before some other owner endings.
concepts.note: Kept separately because this form adds a pronunciation distinction.

sourceCards.title: A long “ī” for “my”
sourceCards.takeaway: كِتَابِي means “my book,” with a long final “ī.”

examples.arabic: كِتَابِي
examples.translation: My book
examples.explanation: The ending is read as a long “ee”: kitabi. The “u” you heard in كِتَابُكَ is not pronounced before this ي. Like the other attached owners, “my” makes the noun part of an idafah, without الـ or tanwin.

reviewPrompts.prompt: How do you say “my book”?
reviewPrompts.answer: كِتَابِي, with a long final ī.

sourceCards.title: The object gets an “a” ending here
sourceCards.takeaway: An object’s role can change its ending; possession and adjective agreement still apply.

examples.arabic:
أُحِبُّ اللَّهَ
أُحِبُّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ
أُحِبُّ اللُّغَةَ الْعَرَبِيَّةَ
examples.translation:
I love Allah.
I love the Messenger of Allah.
I love the Arabic language.
examples.explanation: اللَّهَ and رَسُولَ are objects, so each ends in “a” here. In رَسُولَ اللَّهِ, the second word stays majrur because it is a mudaf ilayhi. In اللُّغَةَ الْعَرَبِيَّةَ, the adjective matches its noun’s mansub ending. With “my,” as in أَبِي, this object ending is not visible.

مَاذَا تُحِبُّ؟

examples.translation:

What do you love?
Do you love your language? (one male person)

sourceCards.title: A new relationship word: “after”

examples.arabic:
بَعْدَ الدَّرْسِ
قَبْلَ الصَّلَاةِ
examples.translation:
After the lesson
Before the prayer
examples.explanation: In these phrases, قَبْلَ and بَعْدَ are mudaf, and الدَّرْسِ and الصَّلَاةِ are mudaf ilayhi. This expands the short note on بَعْدَ in Chapter 12.

examples.arabic: بَعْدَ
examples.translation: After
examples.explanation: The vocabulary entry gives the word and its grammar rule, without a full example phrase. Connect it with تَحْتَ, أَمَامَ, خَلْفَ, and عِنْدَ: each links to a following noun through an idafah relationship, so that noun is majrur.

قَبْلَ الصَّلَاةِ
reviewPrompts.answer: قَبْلَ (“before”) and بَعْدَ (“after”) link to a following noun as mudaf; that complement is majrur.
reviewPrompts.translation:

sourceCards.title: Arabic adjectives have plurals too
sourceCards.source: Part A · Point 1 and vocabulary · pp. 31, 34
sourceCards.takeaway: Learn the plural of the description as well as the thing described.

examples.arabic:
مُدَرِّسٌ ← مُدَرِّسُونَ
طَوِيلٌ ← طِوَالٌ
examples.translation:
A teacher → teachers
Tall (singular) → tall (plural)
examples.explanation: A sound plural adds an ending while keeping the main word recognisable. A broken plural changes the internal pattern. Unlike an English adjective such as “tall,” طَوِيلٌ itself has a plural form, طِوَالٌ, given in this chapter’s vocabulary. Learn a word’s plural with its singular.

sourceCards.title: Attach ـهُمْ for “their”
sourceCards.takeaway: Attached to a noun, ـهُمْ means “their.”

examples.arabic:
أَيْنَ بَيْتُهُمْ؟
أَبُوهُمْ تَاجِرٌ شَهِيرٌ
examples.translation:
Where is their house?
Their father is a famous merchant.
examples.explanation: Compare كِتَابُهُ (“his book”) with بَيْتُهُمْ (“their house”). هُمْ stands alone for “they” or attaches for “their”; its job depends on where it appears. أَبُوهُمْ also keeps the special و in this possession form.

sourceCards.title: A feminine plural “they” and “their”
sourceCards.takeaway: هُنَّ for “they”; ـهُنَّ for “their,” referring to females.

examples.arabic:
هُمْ إِخْوَتِي وَهُنَّ أَخَوَاتِي
هُنَّ زَمِيلَاتِي، وَهَذَا بَيْتُهُنَّ
examples.translation:
They are my brothers, and they are my sisters.
They are my female classmates, and this is their house.
examples.explanation: Contrast هُمْ with هُنَّ. The shaddah in هُنَّ doubles the ن. As with هُمْ, the independent and attached forms look alike, but one is the subject “they” and the other expresses ownership.

examples.arabic:
الْكِتَابُ سَهْلٌ
خَرَجَ بِلَالٌ
examples.translation:

examples.arabic:
إِنَّ الْمُدَرِّسَ جَدِيدٌ
إِنَّ آمِنَةَ طَالِبَةٌ
إِنَّ حَامِدًا مَرِيضٌ
examples.translation:

Indeed, Aminah is a student.
Indeed, Hamid is sick.
examples.explanation: الْمُدَرِّسَ keeps no tanwin because of الـ. آمِنَةَ keeps no tanwin because of its name class. حَامِدًا keeps tanwin, now with fathah. The noun is mansub in all three examples, but its spelling reflects its own class.

examples.arabic:
بِلَالٌ ذُو عِلْمٍ وَأُخْتُهُ ذَاتُ خُلُقٍ
هَؤُلَاءِ الطُّلَّابُ ذَوُو خُلُقٍ
هَؤُلَاءِ الطَّالِبَاتُ ذَوَاتُ خُلُقٍ
examples.translation:

These male students are well-mannered.
These female students are well-mannered.
examples.explanation: Use ذُو for masculine singular and ذَاتُ for feminine singular; the plurals here are ذَوُو and ذَوَاتُ. The quality after each form stays in the mudaf-ilayhi relationship.

sourceCards.title: Offer two choices with أَ… أَمْ…
sourceCards.takeaway: Put the question particle next to the first option being compared.

examples.arabic:
أَطَبِيبٌ أَنْتَ أَمْ مُهَنْدِسٌ؟
أَمُدَرِّسٌ أَنْتَ أَمْ طَالِبٌ؟

Are you a teacher or a student?
Did you go to Makkah or Jeddah?
examples.explanation: The Key corrects questions that put أَ before أَنْتَ or the verb while the actual choice is between professions or destinations. Place أَ before one alternative and أَمْ before the other.

sourceCards.title: Hundred and thousand take a singular counted noun
sourceCards.takeaway: Hundred/thousand + singular majrur counted noun.

examples.arabic:
مِائَةُ كِتَابٍ
أَلْفُ رِيَالٍ
أَلْفُ مُسْلِمَةٍ وَمِائَةُ طَالِبَةٍ
examples.translation:

One thousand riyals
One thousand Muslim women and one hundred female students
examples.explanation: The counted-noun pattern differs from Book 1’s 3–10: it is singular here, not plural. The same number forms serve masculine and feminine counted nouns. The ا in the spelling مِائَة is silent; مِئَة is another spelling given by the Key.

sourceCards.title: A kasrah-looking ending need not mean majrur
sourceCards.takeaway: Work out grammatical case from the role, not only the last visible mark.

examples.arabic:
هَذَا الْكِتَابُ غَالٍ
أَنَا مُحَامٍ
أَبِي قَاضٍ
هَذَا وَادٍ
examples.translation:
This book is expensive.
I am a lawyer.
My father is a judge.
This is a valley.
examples.explanation: These are words with an underlying final ي, such as غَالِي and قَاضِي. In the indefinite forms shown, the ي and its dammah are omitted. The tanwin remains on the preceding letter. Their role here is still marfuʿ; more about this noun class comes later.

concepts.title: Say “is not” with لَيْسَ
concepts.rule: لَيْسَ negates the statement; بِـ makes the following predicate noun majrur.
concepts.note: Read this rule with the conditions and examples in its original explanation.

sourceCards.title: Say “is not” with لَيْسَ
sourceCards.takeaway: لَيْسَ negates the statement; بِـ makes the following predicate noun majrur.

examples.arabic: الْبَيْتُ جَدِيدٌ ← لَيْسَ الْبَيْتُ بِجَدِيدٍ
examples.translation: The house is new. → The house is not new.
examples.explanation: الْبَيْتُ is now called ism laysa. بِجَدِيدٍ is khabar laysa. The predicate noun takes a majrur ending after بِـ in this construction. The next card explains a valid alternative without بِـ.

reviewPrompts.answer: لَيْسَ negates the statement; بِـ makes the following predicate noun majrur.

examples.translation: The house is not new.
examples.explanation: Here جَدِيدًا is khabar laysa and is mansub. Compare بِجَدِيدٍ in the main lesson example. The meaning is the same; the visible ending changes with the construction. This alternative is flagged briefly for fuller study later.

sourceCards.takeaway: Feminine topic: لَيْسَتْ; before الـ, connect it with a short “i.”

examples.arabic:
لَيْسَتْ زَيْنَبُ بِمَرِيضَةٍ
لَيْسَتِ السَّيَّارَةُ بِقَدِيمَةٍ

Zaynab is not sick.
The car is not old.
examples.explanation: The second sentence connects as “laysatis-sayyaratu.” This is the same linking adjustment seen in Book 1’s ذَهَبَتِ الْبِنْتُ. The predicate also agrees with the feminine noun: مَرِيضَةٍ or قَدِيمَةٍ.

examples.explanation: This differs from the number-first idafah, such as خَمْسَةُ طُلَّابٍ. The descriptive number is definite here, like the noun it qualifies. The number’s masculine/feminine form still follows the counting pattern taught earlier.

reviewPrompts.prompt: Explain the number and counted-noun pattern, including relevant gender and case rules.
reviewPrompts.arabic:
الطُّلَّابُ الْجُدُدُ الْخَمْسَةُ
الْكُتُبُ الْأَرْبَعَةُ
الْأَخَوَاتُ الْخَمْسُ

sourceCards.title: Name the three root positions

examples.arabic:
فَعَلَ
وَقَفَ · وَزَنَ · وَضَعَ
examples.translation:
The root-position model: fa, ayn, lam
He stopped · he weighed · he placed
examples.explanation: The first radical is called fa, the second ayn and the third lam, even when the actual letters differ. A root containing و or ي is weak (مُعْتَلّ). Weakness in the first position is مِثَال, in the second أَجْوَف, and in the third نَاقِص. Two weak radicals give لَفِيف. These are root classifications, not counts of letters visible in every conjugated form.

concepts.title: Track each noun’s reason for its ending
concepts.rule: In عَلَى مَكْتَبِ الْمُدَرِّسِ, the first noun is majrur after عَلَى; the second is majrur as the idafah complement.
concepts.note: Assumes recognition of عَلَى as a preposition.

sourceCards.title: Two reasons for two “i” endings
sourceCards.takeaway: The first noun follows the preposition; the second follows the possession rule.

examples.arabic: عَلَى مَكْتَبِ الْمُدَرِّسِ
examples.translation: On the teacher’s table
examples.explanation: مَكْتَبِ is majrur because it follows عَلَى, “on.” الْمُدَرِّسِ is majrur because it is the owner in the idafah. مَكْتَبِ is also the first word of that idafah, so it has neither الـ nor tanwin.

reviewPrompts.prompt: Why do both nouns have kasrah in عَلَى مَكْتَبِ الْمُدَرِّسِ?
reviewPrompts.answer: مَكْتَبِ follows عَلَى; الْمُدَرِّسِ is the mudaf ilayhi. The first noun’s own case can change.

concepts.title: Match the adjective’s case to its noun
concepts.rule: A describing adjective takes the case of the noun it describes. In longer phrases, use this to identify which noun is described.
concepts.note: The same adjective-case rule appears in four cards. Examples for ordinary phrases and for choosing between an idafah’s two nouns are preserved.

sourceCards.title: The adjective follows the noun’s case
sourceCards.takeaway: When the noun becomes majrur, its describing adjective becomes majrur too.

sourceCards.title: The ending tells you what is new
sourceCards.takeaway: Match the adjective’s case to the noun it describes.

sourceCards.title: An adjective matches grammatical case
sourceCards.takeaway: Check case agreement across the whole noun–adjective phrase.

sourceCards.title: An adjective follows its noun’s case
sourceCards.takeaway: Read the noun and adjective as one related phrase.

examples.arabic:
هَذَا بَيْتٌ جَدِيدٌ
أَنَا فِي بَيْتٍ جَدِيدٍ
مَنْ فِي الْبَيْتِ الْجَدِيدِ؟
examples.translation:
This is a new house.
I am in a new house.
Who is in the new house?
examples.explanation: بَيْتٌ جَدِيدٌ ends in “un” on both words. After فِي, the phrase becomes بَيْتٍ جَدِيدٍ, with “in” on both. In الْبَيْتِ الْجَدِيدِ, both words have الـ and a single kasrah. Gender, definiteness, and case work together.

examples.arabic:
بَيْتُ الْإِمَامِ الْجَدِيدُ
بَيْتُ الْإِمَامِ الْجَدِيدِ
examples.translation:
The imam’s new house
The new imam’s house
examples.explanation: In the first, الْجَدِيدُ matches بَيْتُ in case. In the second, الْجَدِيدِ matches الْإِمَامِ, the majrur owner. Both descriptions are definite, but their last vowels tell you which noun they qualify.

examples.arabic:
الْمُدَرِّسُ الْجَدِيدُ فِي الْفَصْلِ.
سَأَلْتُ الْمُدَرِّسَ الْجَدِيدَ.
قُلْتُ لِلْمُدَرِّسِ الْجَدِيدِ.
examples.translation:
The new teacher is in the classroom.
I asked the new teacher.
I spoke to the new teacher.
examples.explanation: Both words are marfu in the first sentence, mansub in the second, and majrur in the third. The adjective follows the noun’s case even though it does not itself immediately follow the governing verb or preposition.

examples.arabic:
أَحَضَرَ الطَّالِبُ الْجَدِيدُ؟
يَطْلُبُ الْمُدِيرُ الطَّالِبَ الْجَدِيدَ.
هَذَا دَفْتَرُ الطَّالِبِ الْجَدِيدِ.
examples.translation:
Did the new student attend?
The headmaster wants the new student.
This is the new student’s notebook.
examples.explanation: The naat الْجَدِيد follows the manut الطَّالِب in raf, nasb and jarr. Its case depends on the described noun; it does not acquire an independent sentence role as a second subject or object.

reviewPrompts.prompt: In بَيْتُ الْإِمَامِ الْجَدِيدِ, is the house or the imam new?
reviewPrompts.answer: The imam. الْجَدِيدِ agrees with majrur الْإِمَامِ. With الْجَدِيدُ, the house is new.

هَذَا قَلَمِي أَنَا
ذَلِكَ كِتَابُهَا هِيَ

concepts.title: Extend agreement to non-human plurals
concepts.rule: In the basic rule taught here, non-human plurals take feminine singular agreement: كُتُبٌ جَدِيدَةٌ.
concepts.note: Two complementary steps—recognize the class, then apply its agreement. Assumes basic singular/plural recognition; exceptions remain in later source cards.

sourceCards.title: People and non-human plurals behave differently
sourceCards.takeaway: Identify whether the plural refers to people or to non-human things.

sourceCards.title: Treat non-human plurals as feminine singular
sourceCards.takeaway: Non-human plural meaning can take feminine singular Arabic agreement.

examples.arabic: هَؤُلَاءِ طُلَّابٌ جُدُدٌ، هُمْ صِغَارٌ
examples.translation: These are new students; they are small.
examples.explanation: Humans, angels, and similar beings belong to the first class. Things, animals, and concepts belong to the second. Human plurals use plural agreement, as in هَؤُلَاءِ, هُمْ, جُدُدٌ, and صِغَارٌ here. The important new difference is in the plural.

examples.arabic:
هَذَا كِتَابٌ جَدِيدٌ، هُوَ صَغِيرٌ
هَذِهِ كُتُبٌ جَدِيدَةٌ، هِيَ صَغِيرَةٌ
examples.translation:
This is a new book; it is small.
These are new books; they are small.
examples.explanation: كُتُبٌ is plural, but the demonstrative is هَذِهِ, the adjective جَدِيدَةٌ is feminine singular, and the pronoun is هِيَ. English naturally uses “these” and “they” in the translation. This is the basic rule; the Key notes that exceptions are learned later.

reviewPrompts.prompt: Choose: كُتُبٌ جَدِيدٌ, كُتُبٌ جَدِيدَةٌ, or كُتُبٌ جُدُدٌ for the basic rule here.
reviewPrompts.answer: كُتُبٌ جَدِيدَةٌ. كُتُبٌ is a non-human plural; its adjective is feminine singular.

مَا خَرَجْتُ مِنَ الْبَيْتِ لِأَنَّ الْجَوَّ بَارِدٌ
ذَهَبَ إِبْرَاهِيمُ إِلَى الْمُسْتَشْفَى لِأَنَّهُ مَرِيضٌ

concepts.title: Name the hopeful and fearful uses of لَعَلَّ
concepts.rule: With لَعَلَّ, a welcome possibility expresses hope; an unwelcome possibility expresses concern. Context decides the meaning.
concepts.note: Both cards explain the same contrast. The introductory particle-government lesson remains separate.

sourceCards.title: Name the hopeful and fearful uses of لَعَلَّ
sourceCards.takeaway: Use context to decide whether لَعَلَّ expresses hope or concern.

sourceCards.title: Review hope and concern with لَعَلَّ
sourceCards.takeaway: Decide the meaning from what the speaker welcomes or fears.

examples.arabic: لَعَلَّهُ يَرْجِعُ الْيَوْمَ مُتَأَخِّرًا
examples.translation: I am afraid he will come back late today.
examples.explanation: Hope is called التَّرَجِّي; apprehension is called الْإِشْفَاقُ. In this example, coming back late is the unwelcome possibility. The present-future verb يَرْجِعُ fits the possible future event. The grammatical behaviour of لَعَلَّ remains the same.

examples.arabic:
لَعَلَّهُ بِخَيْرٍ.
لَعَلَّهُ مَرِيضٌ.
لَعَلِّي لَا أَحُجُّ بَعْدَ عَامِي هَذَا.
examples.translation:
I hope he is well.
I am afraid he is sick.
I am afraid I will not perform hajj after this year of mine.
examples.explanation: A welcome possibility expresses hope (التَّرَجِّي); an unwelcome possibility expresses concern (الْإِشْفَاق). The last example is the Key’s hadith illustration of concern. The particle’s grammar remains the same in both meanings.

reviewPrompts.answer: With لَعَلَّ, a welcome possibility expresses hope; an unwelcome possibility expresses concern. Context decides the meaning.
reviewPrompts.translation: I am afraid he will come back late today.

concepts.rule: Use سَـ to mark the future explicitly in these statements.

sourceCards.title: سَـ makes the future meaning explicit
sourceCards.takeaway: Use سَـ to mark the future explicitly in these statements.

examples.arabic:
سَيَذْهَبُ أَبِي إِلَى مَكَّةَ غَدًا
سَأَكْتُبُ لَكَ رِسَالَةً إِنْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ
مَتَى تَذْهَبُ إِلَى الْهِنْدِ؟
examples.translation:
My father will go to Makkah tomorrow.
I will write you a letter, God willing.
When will you go to India?
examples.explanation: سَـ is called حَرْفُ الِاسْتِقْبَالِ, the particle of futurity. In the question pattern practised by this Key, the future meaning is expressed without سَـ, as in مَتَى تَذْهَبُ. Do not assume a future translation always requires adding it.

sourceCards.title: A verbal noun behaves like a noun
sourceCards.takeaway: Apply noun rules to a maṣdar, including case and idafah.

examples.arabic:
الدُّخُولُ مَمْنُوعٌ
الرُّكُوعُ قَبْلَ السُّجُودِ
خَرَجْنَا مِنَ الْفَصْلِ قَبْلَ خُرُوجِ الْمُدَرِّسِ
examples.translation:
Entry is forbidden.
Bowing is before prostration.
We left the classroom before the teacher’s exit.
examples.explanation: خُرُوجِ is majrur after قَبْلَ and is itself a mudaf before الْمُدَرِّسِ. The first two examples use الـ on the verbal nouns. The action meaning does not stop a maṣdar from having ordinary noun grammar.

examples.arabic:
أَنَا مِنْ أَلْمَانِيَا. أَمَّا بِلَالٌ فَهُوَ مِنْ بَاكِسْتَانَ، وَأَمَّا إِبْرَاهِيمُ فَهُوَ مِنَ الْيَابَانِ
أَمَّا أَخِي فَيَسْكُنُ مَعَ أَبِي وَأُمِّي
examples.translation:
I am from Germany. As for Bilal, he is from Pakistan; as for Ibrahim, he is from Japan.
As for my brother, he lives with my father and mother.

sourceCards.takeaway: Mansub can mark when an action occurs, not only its object.

examples.arabic:
رَجَعَ بِلَالٌ يَوْمَ السَّبْتِ
ذَهَبْتُ إِلَى السُّوقِ صَبَاحًا
رَجَعْتُ مِنَ الْجَامِعَةِ مَسَاءً
examples.translation:
Bilal returned on Saturday.
I went to the market in the morning.
I returned from the university in the evening.
examples.explanation: يَوْمَ, صَبَاحًا, and مَسَاءً tell you the time of the action, rather than the thing receiving it. English adds words such as “on” or “in,” but these Arabic examples use a mansub time expression.

examples.arabic:
أَذْهَبُ إِلَى الْمَكْتَبَةِ كُلَّ يَوْمٍ
سَأَذْهَبُ إِلَى الطَّائِفِ يَوْمَ الْخَمِيسِ
أَيْنَ تَذْهَبُ هَذَا الْمَسَاءَ؟
examples.translation:
I go to the library every day.
I will go to Taif on Thursday.
Where will you go this evening?
examples.explanation: كُلَّ is mansub as the time expression and يَوْمٍ is its mudaf ilayhi. Likewise يَوْمَ is mansub while الْخَمِيسِ is majrur. In “this evening,” the noun الْمَسَاءَ shows the mansub case of the demonstrative phrase.

examples.arabic: تَكْتُبُ ← كْتُبْ ← اُكْتُبْ
examples.translation: You write → intermediate stem → Write!
examples.explanation: For this basic masculine singular pattern, start with the second-person present-future form. Remove its initial تَ and replace the final short u with sukun. examples.arabic:
اِشْرَبِ الْمَاءَ
اِفْتَحِ الْبَابَ
خُذِ الْكِتَابَ
examples.translation:
Drink the water!
Open the door!
Take the book!
examples.explanation: The isolated commands are اِشْرَبْ, اِفْتَحْ and خُذْ. When joined to الْـ here, the opening hamza is not pronounced. A kasrah on the command’s final consonant prevents two vowelless consonants from meeting: الْتِقَاءُ السَّاكِنَيْنِ. This is a joining adjustment.

examples.translation:

sourceCards.title: An indefinite topic after a question particle
sourceCards.takeaway: After an interrogative particle, an indefinite noun can serve as the topic in this pattern.

examples.arabic:
أَعَقْرَبٌ فِي الْفَصْلِ؟
أَإِلَهٌ مَعَ اللَّهِ؟
examples.translation:
Is there a scorpion in the classroom?
Is there a god with Allah?
examples.explanation: The question particle أَ precedes an indefinite noun: عَقْرَبٌ or إِلَهٌ. That noun can be the mubtada here. The following phrase supplies the predicate. Keep the noun marfu, as the final ـٌ shows; being indefinite does not itself make it an object.

concepts.rule: Read فَإِنَّ here as the reason for the instruction.
concepts.note: Read this rule with the conditions and examples in its original explanation.

sourceCards.title: Give a reason with فَإِنَّ
sourceCards.takeaway: Read فَإِنَّ here as the reason for the instruction.

examples.arabic:
كُلْ هَذَا فَإِنَّكَ جَوْعَانُ
اُدْخُلْ فَإِنَّ الدَّرْسَ قَدْ بَدَأَ
اِغْسِلِ الْقَمِيصَ فَإِنَّهُ وَسِخٌ
examples.translation:
Eat this, because you are hungry.
Come in, for the lesson has already started.
Wash the shirt, for it is dirty.
examples.explanation: The instruction comes first; فَإِنَّ then explains why. The familiar grammar of إِنَّ still applies: الدَّرْسَ is its mansub noun, or an attached pronoun supplies its noun, as in إِنَّكَ and إِنَّهُ. Compare this way of giving a reason with لِأَنَّ from earlier lessons.

concepts.rule: لَا تَذْهَبُ is a statement; لَا تَذْهَبْ is an instruction.
concepts.note: Read this rule with the conditions and examples in its original explanation.

sourceCards.title: “You don’t go” versus “Don’t go!”
sourceCards.takeaway: لَا تَذْهَبُ is a statement; لَا تَذْهَبْ is an instruction.

examples.arabic:
تَذْهَبُ
لَا تَذْهَبُ
لَا تَذْهَبْ
examples.translation:
You go.
You do not go.
Do not go!
examples.explanation: Negative لَا النَّافِيَةُ states that an action does not happen. Prohibitive لَا النَّاهِيَةُ tells someone not to do it. In this regular masculine singular example, the prohibition replaces the final dammah with sukun. Compare the ending carefully: the meaning changes even though the consonants look the same.

You do not go.

sourceCards.title: Use prohibitions in everyday instructions
sourceCards.takeaway: Recognise the prohibition even when connected speech adds a linking vowel.

examples.arabic:
لَا تَجْلِسْ هُنَا
لَا تَكْتُبْ بِالْقَلَمِ الْأَحْمَرِ
لَا تَخْرُجْ مِنَ الْفَصْلِ
لَا تَعْبُدِ الشَّيْطَانَ
examples.translation:
Do not sit here!
Do not write with the red pen!
Do not leave the classroom!
Do not worship Satan!
examples.explanation: The first three verbs clearly end with sukun. In the last example, تَعْبُدِ has a linking kasrah before the following hamzat al-wasl, to avoid two vowelless consonants meeting. That pronunciation adjustment does not turn the prohibition into an ordinary negative statement.

concepts.title: Say that something almost happens
concepts.rule: Use كَادَ / يَكَادُ with a mudari verb to express “almost” or “about to.”
concepts.note: Read this rule with the conditions and examples in its original explanation.

sourceCards.title: Say that something almost happens
sourceCards.takeaway: Use كَادَ / يَكَادُ with a mudari verb to express “almost” or “about to.”

examples.arabic:
كَادَ الْوَلَدُ يَضْحَكُ
كَادَ الْمُدَرِّسُ يَخْرُجُ
يَكَادُ الْجَرَسُ يَرِنُّ
يَكَادُ الْإِمَامُ يَرْكَعُ
examples.translation:
The boy almost laughed.
The teacher was about to leave.
The bell is about to ring.
The imam is about to bow.
examples.explanation: In the first example, the boy reached the point of laughing but did not laugh. The pattern shown is كَادَ or يَكَادُ, followed by a marfu noun and a present-future verb. Even after past كَادَ, the following action uses the mudari form: يَضْحَكُ or يَخْرُجُ.

يَكَادُ الْإِمَامُ يَرْكَعُ
reviewPrompts.answer: Use كَادَ / يَكَادُ with a mudari verb to express “almost” or “about to.”
reviewPrompts.translation:
The boy almost laughed.
The teacher was about to leave.
The bell is about to ring.
The imam is about to bow.

concepts.note: Read this rule with the conditions and examples in its original explanation.

sourceCards.title: A usual habit or what is happening now?
sourceCards.takeaway: In this lesson’s contrast: لَا for the usual situation; مَا for what is not happening now.

examples.arabic:
لَا أَفْهَمُ الْفَرَنْسِيَّةَ
لَا نَذْهَبُ إِلَى الْمَلْعَبِ يَوْمَ الْجُمُعَةِ
لَا أَشْرَبُ الْقَهْوَةَ
مَا أَشْرَبُ الْقَهْوَةَ
examples.translation:
I do not understand French.
We do not go to the playground on Friday.
I do not drink coffee.
I am not drinking coffee now.
examples.explanation: In the contrast taught here, لَا describes the general habit or usual situation. مَا with the mudari refers to the present moment. These are negative statements, so the verbs retain their normal endings; neither coffee sentence is a command to stop drinking.

sourceCards.title: Why “I eat” begins with آ
sourceCards.takeaway: Write آكُلُ, آخُذُ and آمُرُ with the long opening آ.

examples.arabic:
أَأْكُلُ ← آكُلُ
أَأْخُذُ ← آخُذُ
أَأْمُرُ ← آمُرُ
examples.translation:
Underlying combination → I eat
Underlying combination → I take
Underlying combination → I command
examples.explanation: The first hamza is the “I” prefix; the next belongs to the root and has sukun. The Key shows their combination becoming the long opening ā, written آ with maddah. The forms on the left illustrate the underlying combination, not the spelling to use in an ordinary sentence.

sourceCards.title: Limit the meaning with إِنَّمَا
sourceCards.takeaway: Read إِنَّمَا as restricting the statement: “only.”

examples.arabic:
إِنَّمَا أَنْظُرُ إِلَى الصُّوَرِ
أَنْتَ لَا تَكْتُبُ الدَّرْسَ، إِنَّمَا تَكْتُبُ رِسَالَةً
إِنَّمَا الْأَعْمَالُ بِالنِّيَّاتِ
إِنَّمَا الصَّدَقَاتُ لِلْفُقَرَاءِ
examples.translation:
I am only looking at the pictures.
You are not writing the lesson; you are only writing a letter.
Actions are judged only by intentions.
Charity is only for the poor.
examples.explanation: إِنَّمَا narrows what is being said. In the second example, the contrast tells us what the person is actually writing. Notice الْأَعْمَالُ and الصَّدَقَاتُ keep their marfu endings in the nominal examples; do not automatically apply the mansub noun pattern of إِنَّ alone.

examples.arabic:
مَاذَا تُرِيدُ يَا بِلَالُ؟

concepts.rule: Relative مَا introduces “that which …”, rather than asking a question or making a negative.

sourceCards.title: مَا can mean “what” inside a statement
sourceCards.takeaway: Relative مَا introduces “that which …”, rather than asking a question or making a negative.

examples.arabic:
نَسِيتُ مَا قُلْتَ لِي.
أَشْرَبُ مَا تَشْرَبُ.
لَا أَعْبُدُ مَا تَعْبُدُونَ.
examples.translation:
I forgot what you told me.
I will drink what you drink.
I do not worship what you worship.
examples.explanation: This is مَا الْمَوْصُولَةُ. It is different from question مَا in مَا اسْمُكَ؟ and negative مَا in مَا فَهِمْتُ الدَّرْسَ. The words after relative مَا tell us which thing is meant. Decide its job from the whole sentence, not from the word alone.

reviewPrompts.answer: Relative مَا introduces “that which …”, rather than asking a question or making a negative.
reviewPrompts.translation:
I forgot what you told me.

examples.explanation: With هَذَا الْكِتَابُ, the noun has الْـ. The demonstrative matches the thing pointed to: feminine عُلْبَةُ uses هَذِهِ, and masculine كِتَابُ uses هَذَا. The same order works with a possessive pronoun.

concepts.title: Emphasise “never” in the future with أَبَدًا
concepts.rule: لَنْ … أَبَدًا means “will never …”.
concepts.note: Read this rule with the conditions and examples in its original explanation.

sourceCards.title: Emphasise “never” in the future with أَبَدًا
sourceCards.takeaway: لَنْ … أَبَدًا means “will never …”.

examples.arabic:
لَنْ أَشْرَبَ الْخَمْرَ أَبَدًا.
لَنْ أَكْتُبَ إِلَيْهِ أَبَدًا.

examples.translation:
I will never drink wine.
I will never write to him.
Your language is very difficult; I will never study it.
examples.explanation: لَنْ supplies the negative future meaning, and أَبَدًا adds “ever,” giving “never” together. Keep the verb mansub: أَشْرَبَ, أَكْتُبَ and أَدْرُسَ. Do not treat أَبَدًا alone as the word that negates the verb.

concepts.title: Dual nouns use two case endings
concepts.rule: Dual: ـَانِ for marfu; ـَيْنِ for both mansub and majrur.
concepts.note: Read this rule with the conditions and examples in its original explanation.

sourceCards.title: Dual nouns use two case endings
sourceCards.takeaway: Dual: ـَانِ for marfu; ـَيْنِ for both mansub and majrur.

examples.arabic:
هَذَانِ رِيَالَانِ.
أُرِيدُ رِيَالَيْنِ.
اشْتَرَيْتُهُ بِرِيَالَيْنِ.
examples.translation:
These are two riyals.
I want two riyals.
I bought it for two riyals.
examples.explanation: A normal singular noun can show u, a or i for its three cases. The dual instead changes the long ending: riyālāni when marfu, riyālayni when mansub or majrur. The final nun has kasrah in both endings; that small final vowel alone does not identify the case.

sourceCards.takeaway: The dual ending ـَيْنِ serves two cases; context tells you which one.

examples.arabic:
قَرَأْتُ كِتَابَيْنِ.
رَجَعْتُ بَعْدَ يَوْمَيْنِ.
سَمِعْتُ هَذَا الْخَبَرَ مِنْ إِذَاعَتَيْنِ.
examples.translation:

I returned after two days.
I heard this news from two radio stations.

concepts.rule: Masculine: أَحَدُهُمَا / الْآخَرُ; feminine: إِحْدَاهُمَا / الْأُخْرَى.

examples.arabic:

examples.translation:
I have two brothers: one is a doctor and the other is an engineer.
I have two sisters: one is a teacher and the other is a nurse.

concepts.note: Read this rule with the conditions and examples in its original explanation.

sourceCards.takeaway: لَمْ + majzum mudari means “did not …”.

examples.arabic:
يَذْهَبُ ← لَمْ يَذْهَبْ
تَذْهَبُ ← لَمْ تَذْهَبْ
أَذْهَبُ ← لَمْ أَذْهَبْ

You go / she goes → You / she did not go

We go → We did not go

concepts.title: A majzum verb can have a linking kasrah
concepts.rule: A linking kasrah after لَمْ does not make the verb a majrur noun.

sourceCards.title: A majzum verb can have a linking kasrah
sourceCards.takeaway: A linking kasrah after لَمْ does not make the verb a majrur noun.

examples.arabic:
أَلَمْ تَكْتُبِ الرِّسَالَةَ؟
لَمْ تَحْفَظِ الطَّالِبَةُ الْقُرْآنَ.
examples.translation:
Did you not write the letter?
The female student did not memorise the Quran.
examples.explanation: Alone, the relevant forms end تَكْتُبْ and تَحْفَظْ. Joining to the following الْـ drops its opening hamza and would bring two vowelless consonants together. The linking i avoids الْتِقَاءُ السَّاكِنَيْنِ. The verb is still majzum; this kasrah is a pronunciation adjustment.

sourceCards.title: Say “not yet” with لَمَّا

examples.arabic:
لَمَّا أَشْرَبِ الْقَهْوَةَ.
وَلَمَّا يَدْخُلِ الْإِيمَانُ فِي قُلُوبِكُمْ.

Faith has not yet entered your hearts.
My father went to Makkah and has not yet returned.

Twenty thousand, brother. · I want twenty thousand riyals.
examples.explanation: With an expressed counted noun, the number is mudaf and has no tanwin. When that noun is omitted in these examples, عَشَرَةٌ, أَلْفٍ and أَلْفًا take tanwin. This does not mean every Arabic number can take tanwin: fixed teen compounds and the tens retain their own patterns.

examples.arabic:
الْمَاءُ بَارِدٌ. ← كَانَ الْمَاءُ بَارِدًا.
زَيْنَبُ مَرِيضَةٌ. ← كَانَتْ زَيْنَبُ مَرِيضَةً.

examples.translation:

Zainab is sick. → Zainab was sick.
The weather is fine. → The weather was fine.
examples.explanation: The former mubtada becomes اسم كان and remains marfu. The former khabar becomes خبر كان and is mansub. The new ending belongs to the predicate: بَارِدًا, مَرِيضَةً, جَمِيلًا. Match كَانَ / كَانَتْ to the subject as illustrated.

concepts.title: Another لَمَّا means “when”
concepts.rule: Temporal لَمَّا links past events as “when.” It differs from negative لَمَّا (“not yet”), which governs a majzum mudari.
concepts.note: Combined repeated explanations of the same temporal/negative distinction; kept both sets of examples.

sourceCards.title: Another لَمَّا means “when”
sourceCards.takeaway: Read the following verb to distinguish temporal لَمَّا from negative لَمَّا.

sourceCards.title: Temporal lamma means “when”
sourceCards.takeaway: When plus two past events differs from not-yet plus majzum.

examples.arabic:
لَمَّا سَمِعْتُ الْجَرَسَ دَخَلْتُ الْفَصْلَ.
لَمَّا ذَهَبْتُ إِلَى مَكَّةَ زُرْتُ صَدِيقِي.
عِنْدَمَا أَذْهَبُ إِلَى الْمَسْجِدِ أَجْلِسُ فِي الصَّفِّ الْأَوَّلِ.
examples.translation:
When I heard the bell, I entered the classroom.
When I went to Makkah, I visited my friend.
When I go to the mosque, I sit in the first row.
examples.explanation: The “when” use of لَمَّا taught here accompanies the past verb. For the present-future example, the Key uses عِنْدَمَا. Compare لَمَّا يَرْجِعْ, “he has not yet returned”: that negative لَمَّا takes a majzum mudari and is a different construction.

examples.arabic: لَمَّا سَمِعْتُ الْأَذَانَ ذَهَبْتُ إِلَى الْمَسْجِدِ.
examples.translation: When I heard the adhan, I went to the mosque.
examples.explanation: Lamma al-hiniyyah is a time adverb connecting two past events. It differs from governing لَمَّا meaning “not yet”, which takes a majzum mudari. The following verb form helps identify the construction.

sourceCards.takeaway: For all five forms, presence or omission of nun marks the mood.

examples.arabic:
يُرِيدُ الطَّالِبَانِ أَنْ يَذْهَبَا.
الطَّالِبَانِ لَمْ يَذْهَبَا.
أَتُرِيدَانِ أَنْ تَذْهَبَا يَا أَخَوَانِ؟
أَلَمْ تَذْهَبَا يَا أُخْتَانِ؟
examples.translation:
The two students want to go.
The two students did not go.
Do you two brothers want to go?
Did you two sisters not go?
examples.explanation: The five written patterns are يَفْعَلَانِ, تَفْعَلَانِ, يَفْعَلُونَ, تَفْعَلُونَ and تَفْعَلِينَ, called الْأَفْعَالُ الْخَمْسَةُ. sourceCards.title: The dual command is shared by both genders
sourceCards.source: Point 1 commands and subject pronouns · pp. 90–91
sourceCards.takeaway: Use اِذْهَبَا for either gender when there are two listeners.

examples.arabic:
اِذْهَبَا يَا أَخَوَانِ.
اِذْهَبَا يَا أُخْتَانِ.
هُمَا · أَنْتُمَا · نَحْنُ
examples.translation:

Go, sisters (two)!
They two · you two · we
examples.explanation: هُمَا is the independent third-person dual pronoun for both genders, and أَنْتُمَا is the shared second-person form. The first person uses نَحْنُ. In the attached subject forms, alif appears in ذَهَبَا, ذَهَبَتَا, يَذْهَبَانِ and تَذْهَبَانِ; the past second person uses ـتُمَا.

sourceCards.title: Dual possessors and objects use ـهُمَا and ـكُمَا
sourceCards.takeaway: The dual suffix stays the same across these possessive and object uses.

examples.arabic:
أَبُوهُمَا · أَبُوكُمَا · أَبُونَا
رَأَيْتُهُمَا · رَأَيْتُكُمَا
رَآنَا الْمُدِيرُ.
examples.translation:
Their father (two) · your father (two) · our father
I saw them two · I saw you two
The headmaster saw us.
examples.explanation: The third-person dual suffix is ـهُمَا, and the second-person suffix is ـكُمَا, in both the possessive and object roles shown here. First-person ـنَا serves two or more people. The suffix’s function comes from what it attaches to: a noun gives possession; the illustrated verbs give an object.

concepts.title: Check what the idafah is linked to
concepts.rule: In these ordinary idafahs, a definite complement makes the phrase definite; an indefinite complement leaves it indefinite.
concepts.note: A later refinement, not a duplicate of the introductory possession cards.

sourceCards.title: Idafah takes definiteness from its complement
sourceCards.takeaway: Check the complement, not just the mudaf’s missing tanwin.

examples.arabic:
كِتَابُ هَذَا · كِتَابُ الْمُدَرِّسِ · كِتَابُهُ · كِتَابُ حَامِدٍ
كِتَابُ طَالِبٍ · بَيْتُ مُدَرِّسٍ
examples.translation:
This person’s book · the teacher’s book · his book · Hamid’s book
A student’s book · a teacher’s house
examples.explanation: The first line has definite complements: a demonstrative, an article-bearing noun, a pronoun and a name. The second line has indefinite complements, so its phrases remain indefinite. Omission of tanwin from the mudaf occurs in both lines and does not by itself prove definiteness.

reviewPrompts.prompt: Compare كِتَابُ الْمُدَرِّسِ and كِتَابُ طَالِبٍ. Which is definite?
reviewPrompts.answer: كِتَابُ الْمُدَرِّسِ is definite (“the teacher’s book”). كِتَابُ طَالِبٍ is indefinite (“a student’s book”). Both first nouns lack tanwin.

concepts.title: Finish the idafah before describing the first noun
concepts.rule: An adjective describing the first noun follows the complete idafah. In the definite examples here, that adjective is definite.
concepts.note: Use adjective-case to distinguish description of the thing from description of its owner.

sourceCards.title: Describe a possessed thing after the whole phrase
sourceCards.takeaway: Complete the possession phrase first, then add the first noun’s adjective.

examples.arabic:
بَيْتُ الْإِمَامِ الْجَدِيدُ
بَيْتُهُ الْجَدِيدُ
examples.translation:
The imam’s new house
His new house
examples.explanation: بَيْتُ is definite through its owner, although it has no الـ itself. Its adjective is definite: الْجَدِيدُ. The adjective follows the complete idafah rather than interrupting the link between the thing and its owner.

reviewPrompts.prompt: Say “his new house.”
reviewPrompts.answer: بَيْتُهُ الْجَدِيدُ.

concepts.title: Recognize several ways of being definite
concepts.rule: Personal pronouns, proper names, demonstratives, relative pronouns, and nouns with الـ are definite categories in this source.
concepts.note: An overview of the categories listed on this card, not an exhaustive account of every construction. Relative pronouns can be explored through the source card.

sourceCards.title: Definite nouns identify something specific
sourceCards.takeaway: Definiteness is not the same as having الْـ or lacking tanwin.

examples.arabic:
أَنَا · أَنْتَ · هُوَ
أَحْمَدُ · بِلَالٌ · مَكَّةُ
هَذَا · ذَلِكَ · أُولَئِكَ
الَّذِي · الَّذِينَ · الَّتِي
الْكِتَابُ · الرَّجُلُ
examples.translation:
I · you · he
Ahmad · Bilal · Makkah
This · that · those
Relative pronouns: who/which
The book · the man
examples.explanation: The first five definite categories listed are personal pronouns, proper names, demonstratives, relative pronouns, and nouns bearing الْـ. Relative مَا and مَنْ also belong to the relative category when used in that function. A proper name can take tanwin and still be definite.

reviewPrompts.prompt: Must every definite word begin with الـ? Give a counterexample.
reviewPrompts.answer: No. For example, حَامِدٌ is a definite proper name; أَنَا is a definite personal pronoun.

examples.translation:

I asked the teacher.
This is the teacher’s car.
examples.explanation: The subject is marfu, the object mansub, and the mudaf ilayhi majrur. Dammah, fathah and kasrah are the primary case signs. Other noun groups use secondary signs, so a grammatical case is not simply the name of one visible vowel.

مَا سَأَلْتُ الْمُدَرِّسِينَ.

examples.arabic: قَتَلَ الْفَتَى الْأَفْعَى بِالْعَصَا.

examples.arabic:
يَتْلُو ← لَمْ يَتْلُ
يَبْكِي ← لَمْ يَبْكِ
يَنْسَى ← لَمْ يَنْسَ
أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَمْشِيَ.
أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَتْلُوَ.
أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَنْسَى.
examples.translation:
He recites → he did not recite
He weeps → he did not weep
He forgets → he did not forget
I want to walk.
I want to recite.
I want to forget.
examples.explanation: The marfu u is latent after final ya, waw or alif. In mansub, a is pronounced after ya or waw but remains latent after alif. In majzum, the weak letter drops, shortening the long vowel to the corresponding short one.

examples.arabic:
أُرِيدُ كِتَابًا وَقَلَمًا.
خَرَجَ الزُّبَيْرُ وَحَامِدٌ.
وَاللَّهِ مَا رَأَيْتُهُ.

Zubayr and Hamid went out.
By Allah, I did not see him.

Do you have any question?

The spy was killed.

concepts.note: Read this rule with the conditions and examples in its original explanation.

sourceCards.title: A time noun can be mansub without a preposition
sourceCards.takeaway: An Arabic time expression need not copy English “in” or “on.”

examples.arabic:
وُلِدْتُ عَامَ سَبْعَةٍ وَسِتِّينَ وَتِسْعِمِائَةٍ وَأَلْفٍ لِلْمِيلَادِ.
كُنْتُ فِي مَكَّةَ يَوْمَ الْجُمُعَةِ.
أَيْنَ تَذْهَبُونَ هَذَا الْمَسَاءَ؟
examples.translation:
I was born in 1967 CE.
I was in Makkah on Friday.
Where are you going this evening?
examples.explanation: عَامَ and يَوْمَ give the time and are mansub. They have no tanwin when mudaf to the expression following them. In هَذَا الْمَسَاءَ, the demonstrative occupies the time position and the following noun shows nasb. The date example names the CE calendar.

examples.explanation: The command of أَتَى يَأْتِي begins underlyingly with two hamzas. At the beginning of speech, vowelled hamza plus sakin hamza becomes long ī. examples.arabic:
يَجِبُ عَلَيْهِ أَنْ لَا يَخْرُجَ مِنَ الْفَصْلِ.
لَا يَجِبُ عَلَيْنَا أَنْ نَحْضُرَ هَذَا الدَّرْسَ.

He should not leave the classroom.
We need not attend this lesson.

الْقِرَاءَةُ مُفِيدَةٌ.
نَحْنُ طُلَّابٌ.

sourceCards.source: Indefinite topic a and footnotes · p. 51

examples.arabic:
فِي الْغُرْفَةِ رَجُلٌ.
لِي أَخٌ.
تَحْتَ الْمَكْتَبِ سَاعَةٌ.
عِنْدَنَا سَيَّارَةٌ.
examples.translation:
There is a man in the room.
I have a brother.
There is a watch under the desk.
We have a car.
examples.explanation: A shibh jumlah predicate is either a prepositional phrase or a zarf expression. With the indefinite topic in this construction, it comes first. تَحْت and عِنْد are Arabic nouns, not preposition particles: their following nouns are mudaf ilayhi. Reversing the first example can produce a descriptive phrase rather than the intended complete statement.

مَا بِكَ؟
مَنْ مَرِيضٌ؟
كَمْ طَالِبًا فِي الْفَصْلِ؟
examples.translation:

How many students are in the classroom?

examples.arabic:
أَنْتَ مُدَرِّسٌ. ← أَمُدَرِّسٌ أَنْتَ؟
عَجِيبٌ هَذَا.
مَنْ مَرِيضٌ؟ · مَا اسْمُكَ؟
فِي الْمَسْجِدِ رِجَالٌ.
examples.translation:
You are a teacher. → Are you a teacher?
This is strange.
Who is sick? · What is your name?
There are men in the mosque.
examples.explanation: A normal definite topic usually comes first, but a predicate can be fronted. لَوِ اجْتَهَدْتَ لَنَجَحْتَ.
لَوْ عَرَفْتُ أَنَّكَ مَرِيضٌ مَا تَأَخَّرْتُ.
لَوْ سَمِعْتَ قِصَّتَهُ لَبَكَيْتَ.
examples.translation:
Had you worked hard, you would have passed.
Had I known you were sick, I would not have been late.
Had you heard his story, you would have cried.
examples.explanation: The first example implies the effort and result did not occur. The second clause is the jawab, commonly introduced by lam in an affirmative result. وَإِنْ تَعُودُوا نَعُدْ.
وَإِنْ عُدْتُمْ عُدْنَا.
مَنْ كَانَ يُرِيدُ حَرْثَ الْآخِرَةِ نَزِدْ لَهُ فِي حَرْثِهِ.

If you return, We shall return.
If you return, We shall return.
Whoever desires the harvest of the Hereafter, We increase it for him.
Whoever stands in prayer on the Night of Qadr with faith and hope of reward will have past sins forgiven.
examples.explanation: Both verbs may be mudari, both madi, or one of each. A mudari in the direct conditional construction is majzum; a madi stays mabni without a new visible mood ending. مَنْ لَبِسَ الْحَرِيرَ فِي الدُّنْيَا فَلَنْ يَلْبَسَهُ فِي الْآخِرَةِ.

سَتَفْهَمُ هَذَا يَوْمًا مَا.
examples.translation:
Give me some book.
I saw him somewhere.
You will understand this someday.
examples.explanation: The Key calls this the completely indefinite and vague ma. It follows the noun as an adjective-like qualifier: a certain book, place, day or reason. It is not the negative ma or a question asking “what?”.

concepts.title: Separate direct objects from subjects
concepts.rule: Ask who does the action, then whether it directly affects an object.
concepts.note: Read this rule with the conditions and examples in its original explanation.

sourceCards.title: Separate direct objects from subjects
sourceCards.takeaway: Ask who does the action, then whether it directly affects an object.

examples.arabic:
قَتَلَ الْجُنْدِيُّ الْجَاسُوسَ.
فَرِحَ الْمُدَرِّسُ.
خَرَجَ الطُّلَّابُ.
examples.translation:
The soldier killed the spy.
The teacher was happy.
The students went out.
examples.explanation: A mutaaddi verb takes a direct object: the soldier is fail and the spy maful bihi. A lazim verb such as فَرِحَ or خَرَجَ does not need a direct object. Do not label the subject as an object just because it experiences a change.

Liked the thing · disliked the thing

concepts.note: Read this rule with the conditions and examples in its original explanation.

sourceCards.title: Forms II and IV can make an action causative
sourceCards.takeaway: A useful causative pattern is not a licence to invent either form for every root.

examples.arabic:
نَزَلْتُ مِنَ السَّيَّارَةِ ثُمَّ نَزَّلْتُ الطِّفْلَ.
جَلَسْتُ فِي الصَّفِّ الْأَوَّلِ وَأَجْلَسْتُ الطِّفْلَ بِجَانِبِي.
examples.translation:
I got out of the car, then took the child down.
I sat in the first row and seated the child beside me.
examples.explanation: Doubling the middle radical is tadif; Form IV’s added hamza is the transitive hamza. Some roots use both forms, such as نَزَّلَ and أَنْزَلَ; most use one. The Key says to learn the actual choice from books and dictionaries.

examples.arabic:
فَتَحْتُ الْبَابَ.
فَتَّحْتُ أَبْوَابَ الْفُصُولِ.
عَدَّدَ الرَّجُلُ مَالَهُ.
examples.translation:
I opened the door.
I opened the classroom doors.
The man repeatedly counted his money.
examples.explanation: The action may affect many objects or one object many times. The Key contrasts this extensive meaning with ordinary فتح and عد. It is another Form II use alongside causative meaning.

examples.arabic:
كَسَرْتُ الْكُوبَ. ← كَسَّرْتُ الْكُوبَ.
قَطَعْتُ الْحَبْلَ. ← قَطَّعْتُ الْحَبْلَ.
examples.translation:
I broke the glass → smashed it.
I cut the rope → cut it to pieces.
examples.explanation: The Key distinguishes thorough or forceful action on one object from extensive action affecting many objects or repeated occasions. Both can use the same doubled pattern. The lexical meaning and context select the reading.

examples.arabic:
جَاءَ الْمُدَرِّسُ لَكِنِ الطُّلَّابُ مَا جَاءُوا.
غَابَ عَلِيٌّ وَلَكِنْ حَضَرَ أَحْمَدُ.
examples.translation:
The teacher came, but the students did not.
Ali was absent, but Ahmad attended.
examples.explanation: لَكِنَّ is a sister of inna and makes its ism mansub. لَكِنْ, without doubled nun, does not do this: الطُّلَّابُ stays marfu. Light lakin may also introduce a verbal sentence. The linking kasrah before al does not restore shaddah or government.

examples.arabic:
كَسَرْتُ الْكُوبَ. ← اِنْكَسَرَ الْكُوبُ.
كَسَّرْتُ الزُّجَاجَ. ← تَكَسَّرَ الزُّجَاجُ.
examples.translation:
I broke the tumbler → the tumbler broke.
I smashed the glass → the glass broke to pieces.
examples.explanation: This is mutawaa. Form VII commonly pairs with the basic فَعَلَ, while Form V pairs with Form II فَعَّلَ. In each result sentence the formerly mansub object is now a marfu fail. These are active-form result verbs, not the morphological passive.

examples.arabic:
لَوْلَا الشَّمْسُ لَهَلَكَتِ الْأَرْضُ.
لَوْلَا الِاخْتِبَارُ مَا حَضَرْتُ الْيَوْمَ.
examples.translation:
But for the sun, the earth would have perished.
But for the test, I would not have attended today.
examples.explanation: The noun after lawla is a mubtada whose predicate is omitted. Its answer here is a past verbal sentence. An affirmative answer takes lam; a negative answer does not. The stated preventing fact exists, unlike a simple unreal “if” premise.

examples.arabic:
مَنْ إِبْرَاهِيمُ هَذَا؟
سَيَّارَةُ الْمُدِيرِ هَذِهِ جَمِيلَةٌ.
أَرِنِي سَاعَتَكَ هَذِهِ.
examples.translation:
Who is this Ibrahim?
This car of the headmaster is beautiful.
Show me this watch of yours.
examples.explanation: The Key analyses the following demonstrative as a naat. It describes the proper name or the whole possessed noun phrase; it does not break the idafah by inserting itself between its parts. The cited فَأَلْقِهْ uses the shortened object-pronoun pronunciation noted in the footnote.

examples.arabic:
خَرَجْتُ فَإِذَا شُرْطِيٌّ بِالْبَابِ.
دَخَلْتُ الْغُرْفَةَ فَإِذَا حَيَّةٌ عَلَى السَّرِيرِ.
examples.translation:
I went out and, to my surprise, a policeman was at the door.
I entered the room and unexpectedly found a snake on the bed.
examples.explanation: Idha al-fujaiyyah presents an unexpected state. Fa is usually prefixed, and the following mubtada may be indefinite, as شرطي and حية are here. There is no conditional premise awaiting an answer.

The boy came to me crying.
Do not eat when you are full.

examples.arabic:
وَصَلَ الضُّيُوفُ إِلَّا أَمْتِعَتَهُمْ.
مَا جَاءَ إِلَّا حَامِدٌ.
examples.translation:
The guests arrived, but their baggage did not.
No one came except Hamid.
examples.explanation: A connected exception excludes a member of the group; a disconnected exception contrasts another kind, such as baggage with guests. Separately, a complete exception names the original group; mufarragh omits it. The latter occurs with negation, prohibition or questioning.

وَاللَّهِ لَأُحِبُّكَ.
